title: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus Uveitis: Onset and Complications
condition_or_topic: Uveitis associated with herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO)
clinical_background: HZO results from varicella-zoster virus reactivation in the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve and causes a painful vesicular rash. Eye involvement occurs in over half of cases and commonly includes conjunctivitis, keratitis, or uveitis. Subsequent complications, including corneal scarring, glaucoma, and recurrent inflammation, can cause temporary or permanent vision loss. A prior population-based study noted that ocular involvement may be absent at the first ophthalmic visit and that complications can emerge weeks or months later, but did not establish their specific timing.
objectives: Determine the proportion of individuals with HZO who develop uveitis and the interval between HZO onset and uveitis diagnosis.
Examine patient characteristics, clinical presentation, and complications associated with HZO uveitis.
Assess whether prompt antiviral treatment influences outcomes.
clinical_question: Among individuals with HZO who develop uveitis (Patient), is prompt antiviral treatment within 72 hours of rash onset (Intervention), compared with no prompt antiviral treatment (Comparator), associated with different frequencies of ocular complications and vision loss (Outcome)?
study_design: Retrospective cohort study of individuals evaluated for acute HZO at the Auckland District Health Board between January 1, 2006, and December 31, 2016.

population.description: Individuals with a first episode of HZO, a characteristic shingles rash in the V1 distribution, and an initial ophthalmic examination at the Auckland District Health Board.
inclusion_criteria: First episode of HZO with a characteristic shingles rash in the V1 distribution.
Initial ophthalmic examination at the Auckland District Health Board during the study period.
exclusion_criteria: Herpes zoster without the characteristic shingles rash.
Atypical presentation or uncertain HZO diagnosis, including an eventual alternative diagnosis.
Initial ophthalmic assessment at another eye clinic followed by referral.
Initial HZO episode or presentation outside the study period.
population.care_setting: Emergency eye clinic within the ophthalmology service of the Auckland District Health Board, Auckland, New Zealand.

interventions: Observed use of systemic antiviral therapy with acyclovir or valacyclovir; treatment begun ≤72 hours after rash onset was classified as prompt antiviral therapy.
comparators: Individuals who developed uveitis versus those who did not.
Among individuals with uveitis, those who received prompt antiviral therapy versus those who did not.

primary: Proportion of individuals who developed uveitis.
Time from HZO rash onset to uveitis diagnosis.
secondary: Demographic characteristics associated with uveitis and clinical features at presentation.
Complications among individuals with uveitis, including visual loss, corneal complications, elevated intraocular pressure, glaucomatous optic neuropathy, and cataract.

Association of prompt antiviral therapy with outcomes. Moderate visual loss was defined as BCVA ≤ 20/50 and severe visual loss as vision ≤ 20/200; visual loss was also classified by whether it was permanent and attributable to HZO.

statistical_methods: Data were recorded in Excel and analyzed using Stata, version 15. Categorical variables were summarized as n (%) and continuous variables as median (interquartile range [IQR]). Continuous variables were compared using the Mann-U-Whitney test and categorical variables using the chi square test. A P value of < .05 was considered significant.
follow_up: Follow-up ended on June 1, 2019, at death, or when care moved to another center. Median follow-up among subjects with uveitis was 5.9 years (IQR 3.5-8.6).
interpretation: Uveitis developed in nearly half of the individuals with acute HZO and in more than half of those with ocular involvement. It was diagnosed most often during the second week after rash onset, and patients without uveitis at an examination in the first week could develop it later. Uveitis was associated with other ocular complications and visual loss, although visual loss in affected eyes is often attributable to accompanying manifestations rather than uveitis itself. Prompt antiviral treatment did not appear to prevent uveitis in this cohort, but among those who developed uveitis it was associated with less permanent moderate visual loss due to HZO (10.9% versus 18.1%, P = .023).
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Smaller studies reported uveitis in 6% to 61% of patients with acute HZO and in 17% to 70% of those with ocular involvement. The authors suggest that differences in referral setting, ethnicity, prior vaccination and ophthalmic examination rates could contribute to this variation. In a prospective study of 64 patients, most uveitis diagnoses occurred at day 1 or week 1 after HZO diagnosis; its timing cannot be directly compared with this study because it was measured from diagnosis rather than rash onset. Corneal involvement affected 73% of patients with uveitis in this cohort, compared with reported keratitis rates of 52%-77% in other studies of zoster-related anterior uveitis. The authors describe their intraocular-pressure findings as similar to a study reporting pressure of 23 mmHg or higher in 40% of eyes with zoster-related uveitis. They also cite prior evidence associating early systemic antivirals with shorter viral shedding, faster lesion healing and less acute pain; a retrospective study from their research group associated early treatment with reduced CVA risk following HZO. A separate claims study found that only approximately 50% of patients received systemic antivirals within 7 days of HZO diagnosis.
clinical_implications: An initial examination without uveitis does not exclude its subsequent development: approximately one in three patients examined in the first week without uveitis (164/542; 30.3%) received the diagnosis at a later visit.

Uveitis can coexist with keratitis and is associated with complications that threaten vision. In this cohort, pressure elevation to 24 mmHg or higher occurred in approximately one-fourth of eyes with uveitis at presentation and one-third at any point; pressure reached 30 mmHg or higher in approximately one-fourth during follow-up.

The association between prompt antiviral treatment and less permanent moderate visual loss in patients with uveitis suggests a possible benefit, without establishing that such treatment prevents uveitis.
practice_implications: For patients with HZO who have no uveitis when examined during the first week after rash onset, clinicians should consider either arranging another examination to assess for later uveitis or explaining the warning symptoms that should prompt the patient to return.

The authors also advise considering a follow-up examination within the first month for patients assessed during the first week, or informing them about uveitis symptoms that should trigger repeat examination.
limitations: The retrospective design has inherent limitations.
Examinations did not follow a fixed schedule after HZO onset, so uveitis might have been detectable before its recorded diagnosis.
The analysis of prompt antiviral treatment did not account for corticosteroid timing or administration, a potential confounder.

Referral bias is possible because some people with HZO might not have been sent for ophthalmic assessment, although the authors note that their clinic receives the vast majority of local referrals for such evaluation.
The study preceded publicly funded shingles vaccination in New Zealand, so its findings may not reflect disease severity in populations with high vaccination rates.
strengths: An eye specialist reviewed all charts of patients with herpes zoster instead of relying on diagnostic codes for data collection.

secondary_results: Of 1010 charts reviewed, 141 patients were excluded: herpes simplex, 26; chickenpox, 9; first episode outside the study period or assessment at another location, 76; herpes zoster sine herpete, 9; non V1 dermatome, 7; uncertain diagnosis, 9; and an alternative diagnosis, 5.

At presentation, 83 subjects (9.6%) were immunosuppressed; disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs were used by 36 (4.1%), oral corticosteroid by 35 (4.0%), and 5 (0.6%) had human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. No subject reported or had a record of previous shingles-prevention vaccination.

Oral or intravenous acyclovir or valacyclovir was started in 765 subjects (88.0%; 741 oral, 24 intravenous followed by oral); it was not used in 95 (10.9%) and was undocumented in 9 (1.0%). The median interval from rash onset to starting oral antiviral therapy was 3 days (IQR 1-5 days). Intravenous antiviral was administered to 24 (2.8%); 468 (53.9%) received antiviral therapy ≤72 hours after rash onset.

The uveitis and no-uveitis groups respectively had median ages of 66.9 (IQR 55.0-77.1) and 63.8 (IQR 50.1-74.1), P = .026; female participants numbered 189 (45.8%) and 224 (49.1%), P = .322. Ethnicity had an overall P value of .520: Caucasian, 301 (72.9%) and 320 (70.2%); Māori, 23 (5.6%) and 19 (4.2%); Pasifika, 23 (5.6%) and 24 (5.3%); Asian, 60 (14.5%) and 72 (15.8%); Other, 3 (0.7%) and 10 (2.2%); Unknown, 3 (0.7%) and 11 (2.4%).

In the uveitis and no-uveitis groups respectively, immunosuppression was present in 45 (10.9%) and 38 (8.3%), P = .199; diabetes in 50 (12.1%) and 52 (11.4%), P = .748. Presenting BCVA was median 20/30 (IQR 20/25-20/50) and median 20/25 (IQR 20/20-20/40), P < .001. Presenting IOP (mmHg) was median 17 (IQR 13-23) and median 14 (IQR 12-18), P < .001; presenting IOP > 24 mmHg occurred in 97 (23.5%) and 15 (3.9%), P < .001.

In the uveitis and no-uveitis groups respectively, lid swelling occurred in 239 (57.9%) and 244 (53.5%), P = .196; conjunctivitis in 368 (89.1%) and 293 (64.3%), P < .001; corneal involvement in 301 (72.9%) and 144 (31.6%), P < .001; pseudodendrites in 174 (42.1%) and 81 (17.8%), P < .001; disciform keratitis in 79 (19.1%) and 23 (5.0%), P < .001; optic neuropathy in 10 (2.4%) and 5 (1.1%), P = .134; and cranial nerve palsy in 21 (5.1%) and 9 (2.0%), P = .012. The baseline table lists Prompt acyclovir as 220 (54.2%) and 248 (54.4.4%), P = .678; the second percentage is printed inconsistently in the article.

For the analysis of presentation timing, 14 individuals were excluded because rash-onset dates were not definitively documented. Initial evaluation occurred on days 0 through 7 in 77.0% (658/855), during the second week in 12.5% (107/855), during the third week in 4.8% (41/855), and after the third week in 5.7% (49/855). Among 197 individuals first examined on day 8 or later, 59.9% had uveitis diagnosed at that visit and 4.6% had it diagnosed later.

By day of initial presentation after rash onset, the number examined, uveitis diagnosed at presentation, and uveitis diagnosed later were: day 0, 22, 1 (4.5%), 13 (59.1); day 1, 51, 5 (9.8%), 15 (29.4%); day 2, 70, 6 (8.6%), 21 (30.0%); day 3, 132, 22 (16.7%), 38 (28.8%); day 4, 99, 12 (12.1%), 22 (22.2%); day 5, 105, 19 (18.1%), 21 (20.0%); day 6, 61, 14 (23.0%), 15 (24.6%); and day 7, 118, 37 (31.6%), 19 (16.1%). The day 0 subsequent-diagnosis entry appears as 13 (59.1), without a percent sign.

By later initial-presentation interval after rash onset, the number examined, uveitis diagnosed at presentation, and uveitis diagnosed later were: days 8-14, 107, 54 (50.5%), 7 (6.5%); days 15-21, 41, 27 (65.9%), 2 (4.9%); and >21 days, 49, 37 (75.5%), 0 (0.0%).
All eyes with uveitis had anterior uveitis except one eye with panuveitis. Median follow-up among subjects with uveitis was 5.9 years (IQR 3.5-8.6).

In the comparison of published studies, the current study's table lists 413 uveitis cases among 869 HZO cases (47.5%) and 737 cases with ocular involvement (56.0%). Its 47.5% entry differs from the 47.6% reported elsewhere in the article for 413 of 869 patients.

The published-study comparison reports: Yawn et al.1, 88 uveitis cases, total HZO NS, and 184 with ocular involvement (47.8%); Szeto et al.4, 46, 259 (17.7%), and 170 (27.1%); Womack et al.8, 37, 86 (43.0%), and 61 (60.7%); Zaal et al.9, 32, 73 (43.8%), and 46 (69.6%); Kahloun et al.10, 31, 51 (60.8%), and 45 (68.9%); Nithyanandam et al.11, 31, 64 (48.4%), and ocular involvement NS; Tran et al.12, 20, 90 (22.2%), and 62 (32.3%); Puri et al.13, 13, 68 (19.1%), and 53 (24.5%); Borkar et al.14, 8, 134 (6.0%), and 47 (17.0%). For each study, the entries give uveitis cases, total HZO with the reported uveitis percentage, and ocular involvement with the reported uveitis percentage, respectively.

main_conclusion: Uveitis affected nearly half of this HZO cohort and was diagnosed most often during the second week after rash onset; it was associated with additional ocular complications and visual loss. Prompt antiviral treatment did not appear to prevent uveitis, but among those who developed it, prompt treatment was associated with less vision loss. The authors advise considering reassessment within the first month, or counseling about symptoms that should prompt another examination, for patients seen during the first week.
narrative_summary:
This retrospective cohort study examined when uveitis was diagnosed after HZO and which complications accompanied it. Of 869 patients, 413 (47.6%) developed uveitis. The median interval from rash onset to diagnosis was 10 days (IQR 6-14), and 93.0% of diagnoses occurred within the first 30 days. Among 658 patients first examined on days 0 through 7, 116/658 (17.6%) had uveitis at that examination and a further 164/658 (24.9%) received the diagnosis later. Thus, an initial examination without uveitis did not exclude its subsequent development.

Compared with patients without uveitis, those with uveitis had more frequent moderate vision loss (102 [24.7%] versus 68 [14.9%]; P < .001), corneal scarring (123 [29.8%] versus 28 [6.1%]; P < .001), and elevated IOP, among other complications. Corneal perforation was the exception to the significant between-group differences. In patients with uveitis, permanent moderate vision loss attributed to HZO was less frequent with prompt antiviral treatment than without it (10.9% versus 18.1%; P = .023). The authors did not find that prompt treatment prevented uveitis onset. Because uveitis was commonly diagnosed after an early visit, they suggest considering a follow-up examination within the first month or explaining which uveitis symptoms should trigger reassessment. Retrospective data and examinations without a fixed schedule limit certainty about the precise onset of uveitis.

document_sections.heading: PURPOSE
document_sections.content: The study aimed to determine when uveitis is diagnosed after herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) begins and how often related complications occur.

document_sections.heading: DESIGN
document_sections.content: The investigators conducted a retrospective cohort study.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The study included people assessed for acute HZO at Auckland District Health Board from 2006 to 2016. Its primary measures were the proportion developing uveitis and the interval from HZO onset to uveitis diagnosis. Secondary measures covered complications of HZO uveitis and associations between outcomes and antiviral treatment started within 72 hours.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Among 869 people with HZO, 413 (47.6%) developed uveitis. The median interval from rash onset to uveitis diagnosis was 10 days (IQR 6-14). Among 658 people first examined on days 0 through 7 after rash onset, 17.6% (116/658) had uveitis at that examination and another 24.9% (164/658) received the diagnosis later. Eyes with uveitis had higher frequencies of moderate or severe visual loss, corneal scarring, neurotrophic keratitis, band keratopathy, corneal melt, elevated intraocular pressure, glaucoma, and cataract (all P < .01). Among eyes with uveitis, prompt antiviral treatment was associated with less moderate visual loss (P = .02).

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: Uveitis affected approximately half of those with HZO and was diagnosed most often in the second week after rash onset. Other ocular complications and visual loss were more likely in eyes that developed uveitis.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: HZO results from reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve and produces a painful vesicular eruption in that dermatome. Ocular involvement can occur in over half of cases; anterior-segment inflammation, including conjunctivitis, keratitis, and uveitis, is particularly frequent. Subsequent corneal scarring, glaucoma, or recurrent inflammation can cause temporary or permanent visual loss. People with HZO are often referred promptly for specialist assessment, but a previously reported population-based study found that ocular disease may not be evident at the first ophthalmic visit. It also reported that complications such as uveitis or elevated intraocular pressure may emerge weeks or months after the initial HZ diagnosis, without specifying their timing. Because clinicians need to recognize when ocular manifestations arise and what complications they may cause, the present study examined uveitis timing, associated complications, and the possible influence of initial antiviral treatment.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: This retrospective cohort study received approval from the Auckland Health Regional Ethics Committee (#000027) and followed the Declaration of Helsinki. Investigators searched discharge paperwork for patients assessed at the Auckland District Health Board emergency eye clinic in Auckland, New Zealand, between January 1, 2006, and December 31, 2016. Follow-up ended on June 1, 2019, at death, or when care moved to another center. Visual-acuity outcomes for this large HZO cohort had been published previously. Eligibility required a first HZO episode with a characteristic shingles rash in the V1 distribution and an initial ophthalmic assessment at the study department. Exclusions covered rash-free HZV sine herpetica, unclear diagnoses, an initial examination elsewhere followed by referral, and initial presentation before the study period.

document_sections.heading: PARTICIPANTS
document_sections.content: Participants had a first HZO episode with a characteristic V1 shingles rash and underwent their initial eye examination at Auckland District Health Board's ophthalmology department. Ocular HZO meant involvement of an eye or globe structure; isolated eyelid involvement or an isolated cranial nerve palsy did not meet that definition. Patients with HZ sine herpete, atypical presentations with uncertain diagnoses, or referral for chronic complications rather than assessment during the initial episode were excluded. Referrals generally came from a general practitioner, urgent care clinic, emergency department, optometrist, or, for hospitalized patients, an inpatient clinician.

document_sections.heading: OUTCOME MEASURES
document_sections.content: Primary outcomes were the proportion developing uveitis and the time from HZO onset to its diagnosis. Secondary outcomes included demographic factors associated with uveitis, clinical presentation, complications among affected patients, and associations with prompt antiviral treatment. Corneal involvement encompassed epithelial keratitis—punctate epitheliopathy, pseudodendritic epitheliopathy, or an epithelial defect—stromal keratitis, or disciform keratitis. Moderate visual loss was defined as bestcorrected visual acuity (BCVA) ≤ 20/50, and severe loss as vision ≤ 20/200. Visual loss was considered permanent and attributable to HZO when acuity had not recovered by the final visit after inflammation resolved; other categories were loss from non-HZO causes and nonpermanent loss, such as that associated with cataract.

document_sections.heading: STATISTICAL ANALYSIS
document_sections.content: Investigators stored data in Excel and performed analyses with Stata, version 15. They expressed categorical variables as n (%) and continuous variables as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR). The Mann-U-Whitney test was used for continuous-variable comparisons and the chi square test for categorical comparisons. Statistical significance was defined as P < .05.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Investigators reviewed 1010 charts and excluded 141 patients: 26 with a final diagnosis of herpes simplex, 9 with chickenpox, 76 whose first episode fell outside the study period or who had been assessed elsewhere, 9 with herpes zoster sine herpete, 7 with a non V1 dermatome, 9 with an uncertain diagnosis, and 5 with another diagnosis. The analysis comprised 869 patients with HZO; 413 (47.6%) developed uveitis. At presentation, 83 (9.6%) were immunosuppressed: 36 (4.1%) used disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, 35 (4.0%) used oral corticosteroid, and 5 (0.6%) had human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. None reported or had documentation of prior shingles-prevention vaccination. Oral or intravenous acyclovir or valacyclovir was initiated in 765 (88.0%; 741 oral, 24 intravenous followed by oral); 95 (10.9%) did not receive antiviral treatment, and its use was undocumented for 9 (1.0%). The median interval from rash onset to starting oral antivirals was 3 days (IQR 1-5 days). Intravenous treatment was given to 24 (2.8%). Treatment began ≤72 hours after rash onset in 468 (53.9%), meeting the study definition of prompt antiviral treatment. Table 1 presents baseline demographic and clinical comparisons. Those who developed uveitis were older and had worse presenting best-corrected visual acuity, higher presenting intraocular pressure, and more corneal involvement and cranial neuropathy. The median time from rash onset to uveitis diagnosis was 10 days (IQR 6-14); Figure 1 depicts diagnosis timing. Table 2 reports diagnoses by day of initial presentation and at later visits. Because rash-onset dates were not definitively documented, 14 people were omitted from that timing analysis. Initial assessment occurred in the first week, days 0 through 7, for 77.0% (658/855); in the second week for 12.5% (107/855); in the third week for 4.8% (41/855); and after the third week for 5.7% (49/855). Among those first seen in the first week, 17.6% (116/658) already had uveitis, while another 24.9% (164/658) were diagnosed on a later visit. Of 197 people initially assessed on day 8 or later, 59.9% had uveitis diagnosed at that assessment and only 4.6% received the diagnosis subsequently. Most uveitis diagnoses (93.0%) occurred within the first 30 days after rash onset. Every affected eye had anterior uveitis except one with panuveitis. Median follow-up among those with uveitis was 5.9 years (IQR 3.5-8.6). Table 3 compares complications by uveitis status: every studied complication was significantly more frequent with uveitis except corneal perforation. Table 4 compares complications among patients with uveitis according to prompt antiviral receipt. Permanent moderate HZO-attributable visual loss (≤20/50) was less frequent with prompt treatment than without it (10.9% v 18.1%, P = .023). The text reports no other significant differences in complication proportions between these treatment groups; Table 4 also marks a difference for overall moderate visual loss (P = .009).

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: In this cohort, uveitis developed in nearly half of those with acute HZO and in over half of those with ocular involvement. Table 5 summarizes smaller published studies, which reported uveitis in 6% to 61% of acute HZO cases or 17% to 70% of cases with ocular involvement. The authors suggest that differences in referral setting could contribute to this variation: referral centers may see a higher proportion of ocular cases than broader health systems. Ethnic composition could also matter, because White ethnicity may be associated with greater disease severity. Prior vaccination rates and the proportion examined by ophthalmologists could likewise affect severity or detection. Some earlier studies may have missed subclinical or minimally symptomatic uveitis that resolved before specialist examination. In the present cohort, patients were predominantly Caucasian and unvaccinated, and every patient underwent slit-lamp assessment by an optometrist, ophthalmologist, or trainee; the authors consider these possible contributors to the observed detection rate. Prior studies associated systemic antiviral initiation <72 hours after rash onset with less time shedding virus, faster lesion healing, and reduced acute pain. A retrospective study by the authors' research group also identified a lower risk of CVA after HZO among recipients of early antivirals. In the present study, permanent moderate HZO-related visual loss (≤20/50) among patients with uveitis was less frequent with prompt antiviral treatment (10.9% v 18.1%, P = .023). The authors report no other significant differences in complication proportions by prompt treatment. They note that, despite evidence suggesting potential benefit, antivirals are often not prescribed after HZO diagnosis: a large U.S. claims study found that only approximately 50% received systemic antivirals within 7 days of diagnosis. Uveitis was diagnosed most frequently in the second week after rash onset. Among people examined in the first week who had no uveitis then, approximately one in three (164/542; 30.3%) received the diagnosis at a later visit. The authors therefore advise clinicians to consider either arranging reassessment for such patients or explaining warning signs of uveitis that should lead them to return. A separate prospective study assessed 64 patients on day 1, week 1, week 2, week 4, month 3, and month 6 after HZO diagnosis, with the first assessment no more than 72 hours after rash onset; most uveitis diagnoses in that study occurred at day 1 or week 1 after diagnosis. Because that study timed events from diagnosis rather than rash onset, its results are not directly comparable. Keratitis can precede, coincide with, or follow uveitis. In this cohort, 73% of patients with uveitis also had epithelial, stromal, or disciform corneal involvement; other studies reported keratitis in 52%-77% of eyes with zoster-related anterior uveitis. Uveitis was associated with visual loss both in this cohort and in another study, although the authors caution that accompanying complications and manifestations, rather than uveitis alone, often account for that loss. Other research associates uveitis at HZO presentation with recurrent and chronic disease. In this cohort, intraocular pressure reached 24 mmHg or higher in approximately onefourth of eyes with uveitis at presentation and one-third at any measured time; it reached 30 mmHg or higher in approximately one-fourth during follow-up. Another study found pressure of 23 mmHg or higher in 40% of eyes with zoster-related uveitis. Pressure can be elevated at presentation or rise in relation to corticosteroid treatment after uveitis therapy begins. In one study, corticosteroid use of 30 days or more was associated with elevated pressure in 92% of herpes zoster eye-disease cases with elevated pressure. Other research identified ocular hypertension as a risk factor for recurrent or chronic eye disease; in one series, secondary glaucoma affected over half of eyes and one fourth of those eyes required trabeculectomy. The authors acknowledge limitations inherent to retrospective data. Examinations did not follow a fixed schedule after HZO onset, so uveitis might have been detectable earlier than the recorded diagnosis. Corticosteroid timing and administration, potential confounders of the prompt-antiviral analysis, were not included in that analysis. Referral bias is possible because some patients may not have received an ophthalmic examination, although the study clinic was the community's sole designated acute eye service for a catchment population of over 1 million and received the vast majority of evaluation referrals. The study preceded availability of a publicly funded shingles-reduction vaccine in New Zealand, so its findings may not reflect disease severity where vaccination is common. The authors identify specialist review of every herpes zoster chart, rather than reliance on diagnostic codes, as a strength. They excluded zoster sine herpete because onset timing cannot be established reliably in those patients. Overall, prompt antiviral treatment did not appear to prevent uveitis onset in this cohort, but it was associated with less visual loss among those who developed uveitis. Because uveitis most often became apparent in the second week and can develop after an examination in the first week, the authors advise considering a follow-up examination within the first month or warning patients about symptoms that should prompt re-examination.
